content_units: Message You Can Send

I get why it can feel that way—mainstream playlists do flatten things a bit, and a lot of pop shares similar production trends. But “all popular music after 2010 sounds the same” doesn’t really hold up once you put a few big songs side by side.
Think about how different these are:
-   Adele – “Rolling in the Deep” (2010)  : big, stomping soul-pop with a raw vocal and almost no glossy club feel.
-   Gotye feat. Kimbra – “Somebody That I Used to Know” (2011)  : sparse, arty indie pop built around an unusual xylophone-like hook and awkward emotional tension.
-   Kendrick Lamar – “Alright” (2015)  : jazz-inflected hip-hop with complex rhythm, social weight, and a completely different vocal approach.
-   The Weeknd – “Blinding Lights” (2019)  : bright synthwave revival, clean and neon, basically built from 80s-style pulse.
-   Billie Eilish – “bad guy” (2019)  : minimal, whispery, off-kilter pop that succeeds by doing less, not more.
-   BTS – “Dynamite” (2020)  : polished disco-pop engineered for lift and bounce.
-   Megan Thee Stallion – “Savage Remix” feat. Beyoncé (2020)  : sharp, rhythmic, swagger-heavy rap with almost no resemblance to Adele or BTS.
-   Glass Animals – “Heat Waves” (2020)  : hazy alt-pop with a dreamy, drifting texture.
-   Zach Bryan – “Something in the Orange” (2022)  : stripped-back country/folk storytelling, intimate and rough-edged.
-   Teddy Swims – “Lose Control” (2023)  : soulful pop-rock with a bluesy vocal and huge emotional crescendos.
That’s soul-pop, indie pop, jazz-rap, synth-pop, minimalist alt-pop, disco-pop, rap, dreamy alt-pop, country-folk, and soul-rock—all in the “popular music after 2010” bucket.

I do think your point is partly fair: streaming, playlist culture, and certain production tools have made some songs converge around familiar beats, vocal effects, and structures. So yes, there are trends. But trends aren’t the same thing as sameness. It’s more accurate to say popular music often shares a few surface features while still being wildly different in rhythm, vocal style, emotion, instrumentation, and genre roots.

A better test might be: if these songs really “all sound the same,” could you honestly confuse   “Rolling in the Deep”   with   “Alright,”   or   “bad guy”   with   “Something in the Orange”  ? Probably not.
5-Song Mini Listening Challenge
Try these back to back, in this order:
1.   Adele – “Rolling in the Deep” (2010)
2.   Kendrick Lamar – “Alright” (2015)
3.   Billie Eilish – “bad guy” (2019)
4.   BTS – “Dynamite” (2020)
5.   Zach Bryan – “Something in the Orange” (2022)
If those sound “basically the same,” then maybe your friend doesn’t dislike post-2010 music—they just dislike pop radio trends.
